briefs.task: Write a short multi-paragraph note, the way someone drafting a status update would. Type real sentences. Then format parts of it: bold a phrase, italicise another, change the size of a selection that already contains MORE THAN ONE size, and use the toolbar rather than shortcuts where you can. Undo and redo some of it. Predict before each action, and read a value BEFORE you change it so you have something to compare against. IMPORTANT — TOGGLE THE SAME CONTROL MORE THAN ONCE ON THE SAME SELECTION. Read doc.runs, then click Bold, then click Bold AGAIN without changing the selection, and predict that doc.runs equals that first reading: a toggle applied twice must return the document to where it started. Do the same for Italic, Underline, and a TEXT COLOUR (click `Text color`, then a swatch, then `Text color` again and the reset entry), and do it at least once on a SUB-RANGE INSIDE an already-styled run rather than on a whole block or a whole paragraph. Try it with the selection made right-to-left as well as left-to-right. This round trip is a property you can predict exactly, and a control that only works in one direction will not show up any other way. FINALLY, TRY `Clear formatting`. It is the reset control and it has never been clicked: read `doc.runs`, style a sub-range (bold plus a colour plus a size), then clear it, and predict `doc.runs` equals the reading you took BEFORE you styled anything. Clearing must REMOVE the properties, not set them to falsy values — a run left holding `italic:false` or `backgroundColor:""` is a different stored state from one that never had them, and `equals` will say so.

Build a document with structure: headings, several paragraphs, and at least two links. Then edit what you built — change a heading's level, retype part of a paragraph, edit a link you already inserted rather than adding a new one, and select across a boundary between two differently-styled runs before formatting. The interesting predictions here are about what a change should and should NOT touch. Then use the BLOCK-LEVEL controls, which no run has touched: `Increase indent` then `Decrease indent`, `Text alignment` set away from the default and back, and `Line spacing` changed and restored. Each is a round trip — read `doc.blockTypes` and `doc.runs` first, and predict the document returns to that reading. Watch particularly whether a block-level change disturbs the INLINE runs it contains, which is a thing it should never do.

Spend MOST of this session on the toolbar controls NOBODY HAS EVER CLICKED, and only enough time on values to have something worth formatting. Read `dom.controls` first. Several of these controls OPEN A MENU rather than acting directly — after you click one, READ `dom.controls` AGAIN, because a menu's entries only exist while it is open and their exact names are what a click target takes. START WITH COLOUR. `Text color` and `Fill color` have never been clicked here, and their shape is where BOTH of this project's filed style defects lived on the document surface: #749 is a toggle that left `italic:false` behind, #793 is a highlight reset that stored `backgroundColor:""` instead of removing it. Each was a control whose OFF state wrote a value rather than clearing one. So: select a cell that HOLDS A VALUE, read `sheet.activeCellStyle`, click `Text color` and pick a swatch, then open `Text color` again and use its reset or default entry — and predict `sheet.activeCellStyle` EQUALS the reading you took BEFORE the swatch. Do the same for `Fill color`. A round trip that leaves an explicit empty string or a falsy value behind instead of REMOVING the key is exactly the defect worth finding, and `equals` will see the difference. THEN the rest of the untouched controls, same shape wherever one has an off state or a default to return to: `Cell borders`, `Horizontal align`, `Vertical align`, `More formats`, `Functions`, `Paint format`, `Create filter`. Read `sheet.activeCellStyle` before and after each, and set alignment away from its default and back. Remember that a clean round trip leaves `sheet.rangeStyles` EMPTY on this surface because the patch is pruned — so predict against `sheet.activeCellStyle` returning to its baseline, and treat any DIFFERENCE as the interesting result rather than the sameness. Do at least one of these on a MULTI-CELL range as well as a single cell. KEEP THE VALUE WORK SHORT — just enough to have something to format. Type a few numbers, add one `=SUM(...)`, then change an input and put it back and predict the dependent cell equals the reading you took before. That round trip has held across many runs: do it once to confirm and move on rather than spending the budget there.

Work with selection and navigation: click cells directly (use the cellCenter reader as a click target), move with arrow keys, Tab and Enter, select ranges, and scroll down to a far row and back. Type into a cell after each kind of movement. The predictions worth making here are about WHERE the edit landed — a keystroke that moves the selection somewhere other than where it says it is, is exactly the class of defect this brief exists to find.
